story.logline: A test kit lands on your doormat; most positive results turn out not to be cancer, yet regular tests catch cancers early, so what does doing every test really change for you?

question: What changes if I do every bowel screening test I'm sent?

source.title: Bowel cancer screening: what the test can and can't tell you
source.publisher: Test fixture written for this repo (numbers are illustrative)
quotes: It is offered every two years to people aged 50 to 74.
Out of 1,000 people aged 50 to 74, about 30 will develop bowel cancer over the next 25 years if none of them is screened.
Over 25 years, screening every two years finds roughly 60% of the cancers that would develop, early enough to treat more easily.
Each time someone does the test, about 5 in 100 get a positive result.
Over many rounds of screening, about a third of people who keep screening will get at least one positive result.
In fact, fewer than 1 in 20 positive results turn out to be cancer.
Missing rounds lets cancers grow without being found.

explain.caption: A test kit lands on your doormat. What does it change?
You take a tiny sample. The test looks for hidden blood.
A positive result means a colonoscopy: a camera check of the bowel.
Many people think a positive result means you probably have cancer.
But most positives aren't cancer. Harmless growths and piles bleed too.
A few colonoscopies find cancer early, when it's easier to treat.
So skip tests, and fewer cancers are found early.
Over 25 years, a hundred people like you split like this.
Back at your door, the next kit is your choice.

simulate.prompt: Change how many tests you do, and your starting risk.

tradeoffs: Each test you do raises your chance of a cancer being found early, and also your chance of a colonoscopy that finds nothing.
A colonoscopy is usually safe but uncomfortable, and carries a small risk.
Skipping a test saves a little effort, but lets a cancer grow without being found.
leftOut: The article says about a third of people who keep screening get at least one positive result. Treating each test as a fresh 5 in 100 chance gives about half after 13 tests, so this page likely shows more false alarms than the article. Positive results often come back in the same people, and the model leaves that out.
Cancers found early are assumed to rise in step with the share of tests you do. The article says regular testing matters more than one test, so skipping tests may cost more than shown.
The model uses one average chance of cancer. Your own risk depends on age, family history and health.
The small risk of a colonoscopy is not counted, because the article gives no figure for it.
The numbers come from an illustrative article. Check the figures for the programme where you live.
The model is for people with no symptoms. If you have symptoms, talk to your doctor whatever your last test said.
